explanation.what_it_is: Omega-3 fatty acids are essential polyunsaturated fats found in fish, algae, and plant sources like flaxseed. The most bioactive forms are EPA (eicosapentaenoic acid) and DHA (docosahexaenoic acid), which your body cannot synthesize on its own.
explanation.how_it_works: Omega-3s are incorporated into cell membranes throughout your body, where they improve cellular fluidity and function. They reduce the production of pro-inflammatory molecules called cytokines and eicosanoids, helping lower systemic inflammation. In the brain, DHA in particular is a structural component of neuronal membranes and supports neurotransmitter function. In blood vessels, omega-3s improve endothelial function, reduce triglycerides, and help prevent clot formation. They also promote a healthier gut microbiome and support muscle protein synthesis when combined with resistance training.

proven_benefits.note: Omega-3s reduce triglycerides, support healthy blood pressure, and lower cardiovascular disease risk across multiple large human studies.
DHA supports memory, attention, and processing speed; evidence is particularly strong for maintenance of cognitive function with age.
Omega-3s measurably lower inflammatory markers like CRP and IL-6 in human studies across diverse populations.
Omega-3s improve gut barrier function and support beneficial bacteria; evidence is solid but less extensive than cardiovascular data.
Omega-3s enhance muscle protein synthesis and support strength gains when combined with resistance training, though effects are modest.

explanation.emerging_research: Recent work explores omega-3s' role in mood regulation, eye health, and bone density, though human evidence remains preliminary in these areas. Some studies suggest omega-3 supplementation may support metabolic health and insulin sensitivity, but larger trials are needed to confirm clinical significance.
explanation.caveats: Quality and EPA/DHA content vary widely among supplements; third-party testing is recommended. Fish oil supplements may cause mild gastrointestinal upset or fishy aftertaste, and very high doses can have mild blood-thinning effects—discuss with a doctor if on anticoagulants.
